extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties (petitioners and patent owners) participating in PTAB inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules applied by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board when deciding inter partes review challenges to patentability (especially obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103), including burdens, claim construction, and admissibility of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner's burden to prove unpatentability in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner has the burden of proving unpatentability of the challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence. 35 U.S.C. § 316(e) (2018); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d) (2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of persuasion never shifts to Patent Owner (Dynamic Drinkware). The trier of fact must find the existence of a fact more probable than not (Concrete Pipe & Prods. of Cal.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity requirement (initial petition)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3) requires petitions to identify 'with particularity . . . the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments or theories not identified in the initial petition may be considered waived (37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b); Intelligent Bio-Sys.). The initial petition must articulate the supporting evidence and reasoning sufficiently to put the Board and parties on notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board institutes an inter partes review when the petitioner shows a reasonable likelihood that it would prevail with respect to at least one of the challenged claims (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution is based on the preliminary record; institution does not resolve the ultimate burden of proof at final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a), obviousness is determined based on underlying factual determinations including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) when in evidence, objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations). (Graham v. John Deere Co.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate obviousness conclusion weighs these fact-findings (Arctic Cat). Consider each factor and the record evidence when deciding § 103(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness determination requires finding 'a motivation to combine accompanied by a reasonable expectation of achieving what is claimed in the patent-at-issue.' (Intelligent Bio‑Sys.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner cannot rely on 'mere conclusory statements' (In re Magnum Oil Tools). The petitioner must articulate a reason why a person of ordinary skill would have combined the references (In re NuVasive). Generic goals like 'to make it better' are insufficient absent a specific reason and expectation of success (ActiveVideo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis is reviewed in view of the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention (Graham). Parties may propose a definition; the Board applies a definition consistent with the cited prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a person having a bachelor's degree in electrical/computer engineering or related subject and two to three years' experience in image/video processing (as proposed in this record). Prior art itself can inform the level of skill (Okajima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed to have 'the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' The Board applies the same claim construction standard used in civil actions under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) following Phillips v. AWH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only terms 'in controversy' need be construed and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Vivid Techs.). Use the specification and prosecution history to inform ordinary meaning. If the ultimate decision does not depend on a particular construction, the Board may decline to construe a term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis and avoiding superfluity in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms with antecedent references must be interpreted consistently so that later occurrences refer back to earlier recitals; constructions that ignore antecedent basis or render claim language superfluous are improper (Process Control; Haemonetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations that read portions of a claim as separate, inconsistent definitions (thereby making parts superfluous) should be rejected. Give effect to all claim language, including 'wherein' clauses that refine previously introduced terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) and nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (e.g., industry praise, long-felt need, commercial success) is considered when in evidence, but such evidence must have a nexus to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A presumption of nexus may be appropriate where multiple patents 'cover essentially the same invention' (Fox Factory), but where claims/patents cover different aspects, the patent owner must show the degree to which the evidence is attributable to the claimed invention. Without a demonstrated nexus, objective indicia do not weigh in favor of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and use of public forum posts / online opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public forum posts (e.g., internet forum comments) that are expressions of opinion can be admissible to show that contemporaneous praise existed, but are not admissible as proof of the factual assertions contained within them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such posts are treated as opinions and may support testimony that praise existed (Cisco Sys.; Quanergy). Distinguish opinion (admissible to show existence of praise) from factual assertions offered for their truth (hearsay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstratives are not evidence and restriction on new arguments at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative exhibits used at the final hearing are aids to oral argument and not evidence. Parties may only rely on evidence previously submitted in the proceeding and may only present arguments previously made in submitted papers; no new evidence or arguments may be presented at the hearing (Paper 43; Consolidated Trial Practice Guide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections to demonstratives that introduce new arguments are proper; the Board relies solely on the written record and admissible evidence, not demonstratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to exclude — moving party burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The moving party (seeking exclusion of evidence) has the burden to establish that it is entitled to the requested relief. 37 C.F.R. § 42.20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the moving party fails to meet its burden, exhibits are not excluded. Motions should specifically identify legal grounds (e.g., hearsay, lack of relevance, unfair prejudice) and point to supporting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert opinion reliance on otherwise inadmissible facts (Fed. R. Evid. 703)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may base opinions on inadmissible facts or data under certain circumstances (Fed. R. Evid. 703), and such reliance alone does not necessarily require exclusion of the expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to expert testimony should explain why the basis renders the opinion inadmissible or unreliable; mere citation to underlying exhibits without legal support is insufficient to exclude expert paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of arguments raised for the first time in reply or at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments first raised in a reply brief (or at hearing without prior presentation) may be waived because the opposing party and the Board lacked a fair opportunity to address them (37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b); Intelligent Bio-Sys.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should include all substantive theories and evidence in their initial filings; newly asserted theories in reply are likely to be deemed waived absent good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness requires more than generic desire to improve
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner cannot satisfy the motivation-to-combine requirement by asserting only a generic desire to improve or replace a reference because it 'would be better'; specific rationale connecting features and a reasonable expectation of success are required (ActiveVideo and related authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how specific features in the prior art would be combined and why that combination would be expected to achieve the claimed result, not merely that one reference 'achieves better image quality' in general terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA versus AIA law based on application filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability law applied depends on the application's filing date. Because the application leading to the '651 patent was filed before March 16, 2013, patentability is governed by the versions of 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 preceding the Leahy‑Smith America Invents Act (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm applicable statutory regime by checking priority and filing dates; apply the correct statutory versions to prior art and obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and weight of later-developed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence developed after the priority date may still be relevant to background, testing methods, or industry practices, but its timing can diminish persuasive weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will admit such evidence if relevant and not unfairly prejudicial; assess persuasive weight in light of timing and consistency with other record evidence (examples: standard-setting/testing documents admitted despite later dates).
